4.7 Ranking Feature Contributions

A valuable aspect of the isoRouting workflow is its computational speed. We can take advantage of this efficiency to rank the individual contribution of each of the 24 engineered features to the upper tail of the anomaly score distribution (S≥0.50S \ge 0.50). Specifically, we evaluate 24 leave-one-out subsets of 23 features each and compare their upper-tail probability mass against the 24-feature baseline (obs_tail_mass_50), categorizing each feature as follows:

  • Positive contribution (Tail Driver): If removing a feature causes the proportion of high anomaly scores to drop (ℙ(S24≥0.50)−ℙ(S−j≥0.50)>0\mathbb{P}(S_{24} \ge 0.50) - \mathbb{P}(S_{-j} \ge 0.50) > 0), that feature actively helps the forest isolate extreme behaviors.
  • Negative contribution (Diluter): If removing a feature causes the proportion of high scores to increase (ℙ(S24≥0.50)−ℙ(S−j≥0.50)<0\mathbb{P}(S_{24} \ge 0.50) - \mathbb{P}(S_{-j} \ge 0.50) < 0), that feature tends to compress the separation between anomalous and normal scores.
Data Preparation: Leave-One-Out Feature Ranking (24 Subsets of 23 Features)
library(dplyr)
library(isotree)
library(parallel)

mat_24 <- as.matrix(df_comp[, vars_24])

# Fit a 500-tree forest on each of the 24 subsets of 23 features
feature_rank_df <- parallel::mclapply(seq_along(vars_24), function(j) {
  sub_mat_23 <- mat_24[, -j, drop = FALSE]
  
  iso_23 <- isolation.forest(
    sub_mat_23, ntrees = 500, sample_size = 256,
    nthreads = 1L, seed = 42, missing_action = "fail"
  )
  sc_23   <- predict(iso_23, sub_mat_23, nthreads = 1L)
  tail_23 <- mean(sc_23 >= 0.50)
  
  tibble(
    Feature      = vars_24[j],
    tail_mass_23 = tail_23,
    delta_tail   = obs_tail_mass_50 - tail_23,
    Effect       = ifelse(obs_tail_mass_50 >= tail_23, "Tail Driver (+)", "Diluter (-)")
  )
}, mc.cores = n_cores) |> bind_rows()

rm(mat_24)
Plot Code: Individual Feature Contributions to Upper-Tail Mass
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(feature_rank_df, aes(x = reorder(Feature, delta_tail), y = delta_tail, color = Effect)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Feature, y = 0, yend = delta_tail), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Diluter (-)" = "#f8766d", "Tail Driver (+)" = "#00bfc4")) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual Feature Contributions to Upper-Tail Probability Mass",
    subtitle = sprintf("Baseline 24-feature tail mass P(S >= 0.50) = %.4f", obs_tail_mass_50),
    x = "Omitted Feature (23 Remaining)",
    y = expression(Delta ~ "Tail Probability Mass: " ~ P(S[24] >= 0.50) - P(S[-j] >= 0.50)),
    color = "Feature Role"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Figure 21 shows that 20 out of the 24 engineered features actively contribute to high anomaly scores in the baseline ensemble. This simple leave-one-out diagnostic illustrates how isoRouting can be used to quickly audit the marginal contribution of each candidate feature.

Next, we proceed with the full set of 24 engineered features to extract and route anomaly archetypes.

5 Archetype Extraction with Engineered Features

We now utilize the 24 engineered features to extract fault archetypes.

5.1 Engine Initialization

We initialize the engine with the engineered-feature YAML configuration and ingest the time course. To avoid scoring the 6-month summer gap as an anomaly, we split the data into baseline_telemetry and stream_telemetry using the major_gap_idx index calculated during initial data validation.

Initialize Engine and Split Data
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(isoRouting)

# 1. Load the package data and configure the engine
data("hvac_features", package = "isoRouting")
config_engineered <- system.file(
  "extdata", "engineered_features.yaml",
  package = "isoRouting",
  mustWork = TRUE
)
engine_engineered <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_engineered)
engine_engineered <- ingest_time_course(engine_engineered, data = hvac_features)

# 2. Retrieve the validated telemetry mapped by the new YAML
hvac_valid_eng <- get_time_course(engine_engineered)

# 3. Bucket 1: Pre-Gap (~40% of data) for baseline archetype extraction
baseline_telemetry <- hvac_valid_eng |> 
  slice(1:major_gap_idx)

# 4. Bucket 2: Post-Gap (~60% of data) for predictive routing evaluation
stream_telemetry <- hvac_valid_eng |> 
  slice((major_gap_idx + 1):n())

5.2 Isolation Forest Training and Score Distribution

Next, we fit the Isolation Forest on baseline_telemetry. The engine pulls the ensemble size (ntrees: 500) and sample size (sample_size: 256) from the YAML configuration.

Fit Isolation Forest
library(dplyr)

# 1. Initialize a baseline-specific engine and ingest only the Winter 2019-2020 data
engine_baseline <- new("DiagnosticEngine", config_path = config_engineered)
engine_baseline <- ingest_time_course(engine_baseline, data = baseline_telemetry)

# 2. Fit the Isolation Forest and extract anomalies 
engine_baseline <- extract_anomalies(engine_baseline)

# 3. Retrieve the scores for the entire baseline dataset
baseline_scores <- stats::predict(engine_baseline@model, engine_baseline@feature_matrix)

baseline_scored <- baseline_telemetry |>
  mutate(anomaly_score = baseline_scores)
Plot Score Distribution
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(baseline_scored, aes(x = anomaly_score)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "#4c72b0", color = "black", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  labs(
    title = "Anomaly Score Distribution",
    subtitle = "Engineered features (Baseline: Winter 2019-2020)",
    x = "Anomaly Score",
    y = "Frequency"
  )

As shown in Figure 22, most baseline observations fall below an anomaly score of 0.50, and the upper tail exhibits two distinct bumps around 0.52 and 0.65. As done with the naive configuration, we use evaluate_k_stability to explore anomaly thresholds by varying the number NN of top-scoring observations retained.

5.3 Threshold Diagnostics

We run evaluate_k_stability to compute the diagnostic profiles across candidate anomaly thresholds.

Run evaluate_k_stability
# Sweep based on size (N)
stability_curve_engineered <- evaluate_k_stability(
  engine_baseline, 
  max_N = 800, 
  min_N = 20, 
  nb_steps = 61, 
  max_k = 10
)

We then plot the profiles using the previously defined wrapper.

Plot Code
# Generate the plot using the previously defined wrapper function
fig_engineered <- plot_topological_stability(
  stability_curve_engineered,
  plot_title = "Anomaly Threshold Diagnostics with Engineered Features",
  plot_subtitle = "Optimal cluster number (k), distance heterogeneity (D), and variable dependency breaks (LID)."
)

print(fig_engineered)

Figure 23 shows that distance heterogeneity (DD) peaks between thresholds 0.590.59 and 0.610.61. Within this interval, Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID) remains elevated before beginning an overall decline.

As done with the naive configuration, we verify that the observed DD and LID values differ from random expectations by sampling sets of NN observations independently of their anomaly scores.

Simulate Engineered Controls
# Generate control quantiles using the engineered engine
lid_control_engineered <- simulate_lid_control(engine_baseline, N = n_sequence, iterations = 100)
dip_control_engineered <- simulate_dip_control(engine_baseline, N = n_sequence, iterations = 100)
Plot Code
fig_dip_null_eng <- plot_baseline_profile(
  dip_control_engineered,
  line_color = "#009E73", 
  plot_title = "Engineered Control: Hartigan's D",
  plot_subtitle = "Expected distance heterogeneity.",
  y_label = "Hartigan's D"
)
print(fig_dip_null_eng)
Plot Code
fig_lid_null_eng <- plot_baseline_profile(
  lid_control_engineered,
  line_color = "#CC79A7", 
  plot_title = "Engineered Control: LID",
  plot_subtitle = "Expected structural dimensionality.",
  y_label = "LID"
)
print(fig_lid_null_eng)

In the engineered diagnostic profile (Figure 23), Hartigan’s DD reaches approximately 0.0450.045 near T=0.60T = 0.60, whereas the 95th percentile of the null control (Figure 24) remains below 0.020.02. This confirms that the observed multimodality reflects distinct anomaly states rather than an artifact of applying Hartigan’s DD to pairwise distances.

The LID control (Figure 25) provides similar confirmation: random subsets fluctuate between 2020 and 2222 dimensions (with a lower bound near 1515), whereas the anomaly subset drops from roughly 10.510.5 to 88 dimensions at T=0.60T = 0.60.

Based on both diagnostics, we select T=0.60T = 0.60 as the anomaly threshold.

5.4 Medoid Extraction

We now extract the cluster medoids (representative anomalies) at T=0.60T = 0.60.

Extract Archetypes at T = 0.6
# 1. Isolate the top anomalies right after Hartigan's D peak
engine_baseline <- extract_medoids(engine_baseline, threshold = 0.6)

# 2. Retrieve the extracted physical archetypes (medoids)
medoids_df <- get_medoids(engine_baseline)

# 3. Print the calibrated k-value
cat("Calibrated k at threshold = 0.6:", engine_baseline@optimal_k, "\n")
Calibrated k at threshold = 0.6: 3

At T=0.60T = 0.60, maximizing the global silhouette score yields k=4k = 4 clusters.

Next, we plot the trajectories of the four medoids using the previously defined wrapper, displaying the context_variables specified in the YAML configuration.

Plot Code
# Retrieve the 10 context variables defined in the YAML
schema <- get_features(engine_baseline)
context_vars <- schema$context_variables

# Generate the plot
fig_medoids_comprehensive <- plot_medoid_trajectories(
  engine_baseline,
  plot_title = "Trajectories of the Four Archetypes at T = 0.6",
  plot_subtitle = "Trajectories of the context variables.",
  label_style = "numeric",
  vars_to_plot = context_vars
)

print(fig_medoids_comprehensive)

Figure 26 reveals four distinct signatures:

  • Archetype 1: Characterized by a dip in t_supply and a simultaneous spike in rh_supply at t=0t = 0, while return variables, outdoor conditions, sp_return, power, and energy remain stable. This profile indicates a brief, unpowered moisture disturbance in the supply air.
  • Archetype 2: Represents a system startup. At t=0t = 0, power and energy step up sharply from near zero, accompanied by rising t_supply and t_return and falling rh_supply and rh_return as the air is heated without added moisture. Setpoint and outdoor variables remain constant.
  • Archetype 3: Captures an unpowered thermal surge. At t=0t = 0, t_supply spikes and remains elevated while rh_supply drops, yet power and energy stay near zero. This decoupling of thermal output from electrical input could reflect an external mechanical fault (such as a leaking heating valve).
  • Archetype 4: Represents a system shutdown. At t=0t = 0, power and energy drop to zero, initiating a steady decay in t_supply and t_return alongside a steady rise in rh_supply and rh_return, while outdoor conditions and the setpoint remain flat.

To quantify which features drive each archetype, isoRouting implements Leave-One-Covariate-Out (LOCO) ablation via method ablate_features. For each medoid, the method replaces one target variable at a time with its global median, recomputes the anomaly score, and ranks features by the resulting score drop.

Run Ablation Tests
ablation_results <- ablate_features(engine_baseline)
Define Ablation Plot Wrapper
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Reusable ablation plotting wrapper
plot_ablation_importance <- function(ablation_df, top_n = 5, plot_title, plot_subtitle) {
  
  # Filter to Top N drivers per cluster and retain raw variable names
  plot_data <- ablation_df |>
    group_by(cluster) |>
    slice_head(n = top_n) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(
      # Create a unique factor for faceted reordering using the raw variable name
      var_ordered = factor(paste(cluster, variable, sep = "__"))
    ) |>
    # Reorder based on the magnitude of the score drop
    mutate(var_ordered = reorder(var_ordered, score_drop))
  
  # Generate the plot
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = score_drop, y = var_ordered, fill = cluster)) +
    geom_col(color = "black", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.8) +
    facet_wrap(~cluster, scales = "free_y") +
    # Strip the cluster prefix to display just the raw variable name
    scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) gsub(".*__", "", x)) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "turbo") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    labs(
      title = plot_title,
      subtitle = plot_subtitle,
      x = "Anomaly Score Drop (Contribution Magnitude)",
      y = "Engineered Feature (Raw)"
    ) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "none",
      strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#f0f0f0", color = "grey80"),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
  
  return(p)
}
Plot Code
fig_ablation <- plot_ablation_importance(
  ablation_results, 
  top_n = 5,
  plot_title = "Medoid Interpretation via Feature Ablation",
  plot_subtitle = "Decrease in anomaly score when feature is reverted to its global median"
)

print(fig_ablation)

The LOCO ablation rankings (Figure 27) confirm the visual trajectory analysis:

  • Archetype 1: Driven primarily by moisture features (d_humidity_delta_15m and humidity_delta), with no power features among the top contributors, confirming an unpowered moisture disturbance.
  • Archetype 2: Led by dw_power, followed by thermal and energy step changes, consistent with a system startup.
  • Archetype 3: Dominated by thermal step changes and saturation margins (d_t_supply_15m, d_supply_margin_15m) without power contributions, confirming an unpowered thermal fault.
  • Archetype 4: Driven by shifts in saturation margins (d_supply_margin_15m, displacement_return_margin) and short-term temperature derivatives, matching a system shutdown.

5.5 Forensic Ledger

Once the cluster count is calibrated and medoids are extracted, we lock in the baseline using commit_ledger(). This method assigns every historical anomaly above the threshold to its nearest medoid based on Isolation Forest tree-assignment Hamming distance.

This cumulative profile tests for progressive wear-and-tear faults, which would manifest as upward-curving trajectories (an increasing occurrence rate over time). Figure 28 shows no progressive degradation:

  • Cluster 4: Occurs once in January, consistent with an isolated system shutdown.
  • Cluster 1: Appears only during autumn and flatlines by December, pointing to a seasonal moisture disturbance.
  • Cluster 3: Accumulates primarily during the coldest winter months, matching its signature of unpowered t_supply surges.
  • Cluster 2: The most frequent archetype, steepening during peak winter (December through February) before tapering off in spring.

Figure 29 clarifies the operational context of each cluster:

Next, we use the cluster radii to examine lower-scoring anomalies.

5.6 Sub-Threshold Anomaly Tracking via Cluster Radii

Analyzing only observations above T=0.60T = 0.60 focuses on severe fault manifestations, whereas early precursors or gradual mechanical wear may develop below that cutoff. To track sub-threshold behavior, we use the cluster radii (Max_Distance) established at T=0.60T = 0.60 as filters.

The route_time_course() method computes the forest Hamming distance between every observation in the scored time course (get_scored_time_course()) and each medoid. Any observation falling within a cluster’s radius is assigned to that archetype regardless of its anomaly score, while observations outside all four radii are labeled "Background".

Route Full Time Course

Figure 30 plots all baseline observations captured within each medoid’s radius (excluding "Background" points). The red dashed line marks the T=0.60T = 0.60 extraction cutoff, while the black curves and grey bands show Generalized Additive Model (GAM) cubic regression spline trends and their 95% confidence intervals.

This view captures system behavior across both high- and low-score regimes without altering the cluster definitions:

  • Effect of a Higher Threshold (T>0.60T > 0.60): Above T=0.64T = 0.64, Cluster 1 (peaking below 0.640.64) and Cluster 4 (0.6050.605) disappear, leaving only the extreme tails of Clusters 2 and 3.
  • Cluster 1: Exhibits a tight band of sub-threshold precursors (scores between 0.490.49 and 0.600.60) during the same autumn window as its above-threshold points, with a flat mean trend near 0.5850.585.
  • Cluster 2: Follows a seasonal arch. Mild occurrences (0.50–0.580.50\text{--}0.58) appear in November before the GAM trend crosses 0.600.60 in December, plateaus near 0.640.64 during peak winter heating (January–February), and subsides in spring. Because the trend declines as outdoor temperatures warm, it reflects seasonal heating load rather than progressive wear.
  • Cluster 3: Most observations sharing this unpowered thermal-surge signature sit below 0.600.60. Its GAM trend remains below the cutoff all winter (drifting from 0.550.55 down to 0.520.52 by April), confirming that the fault does not worsen over time.
  • Cluster 4: Because this singleton cluster has a radius of 00, no sub-threshold observations fall within its boundary and no trend curve is fitted.

6 Predictive Routing and Novelty Detection on Streaming Telemetry

Once the baseline archetypes and their cluster radii (@cluster_radii) are locked inside engine_baseline, the DiagnosticEngine can route new observations without retraining the Isolation Forest or re-running hierarchical clustering.

When new data arrive, predict_stream() projects each observation through the frozen baseline forest (@model), extracts its terminal leaf-node signature (type = "tree_num"), and computes its proportional Hamming distance to each cached medoid signature (@baseline_signatures). Each observation is then classified by combining forest distance and anomaly score:

  1. Known Fault Archetype (Cluster 1 … Cluster k): The observation’s Hamming distance to its nearest medoid falls within that cluster’s baseline radius (d≤Rcd \le R_c).
  2. Background (Background): The observation falls outside all cluster radii (d>Rcd > R_c) and its anomaly score remains below the baseline threshold (S<0.60S < 0.60).
  3. Novel Anomaly (Novel Anomaly): The observation exceeds the anomaly score threshold (S≥0.60S \ge 0.60) and falls outside the radius of every known medoid (d>Rcd > R_c). This flags an unseen fault mode that did not occur during the baseline period.

6.1 Routing the Incoming Stream

Data Preparation: Route and Summarize Streaming Telemetry
library(dplyr)

# Route unseen streaming telemetry using the locked baseline engine
stream_routed <- predict_stream(engine_baseline, new_data = stream_telemetry)

# Lookup vector of baseline cluster radii (returns NA for Background and Novel Anomaly)
radii_lookup <- engine_baseline@cluster_radii

# Summarize the routed states
stream_summary <- stream_routed |>
  group_by(predicted_state) |>
  summarise(
    Occurrences     = n(),
    Median_Score    = round(median(anomaly_score, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Max_Score       = round(max(anomaly_score, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Median_Distance = round(median(distance_to_archetype, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    Cluster_Radius  = round(unname(radii_lookup[first(predicted_state)]), 3),
    .groups         = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(Occurrences))
Table Code
library(knitr)

kable(
  stream_summary,
  caption = "Summary of streaming telemetry routed across baseline archetypes and novelty bounds."
)

Table 6 summarizes the classification of the 16,63416,634 post-gap streaming observations:

  • Background (16,45116,451 occurrences): Nearly 98.9%98.9\% of the incoming stream remains below T=0.60T = 0.60 (maximum score 0.5990.599) and sits outside the baseline cluster radii (median Hamming distance 0.9140.914).
  • Known Archetypes (Cluster 2, Cluster 3, Cluster 1): A total of 166166 observations fall within the radius (d≤Rcd \le R_c) of an established medoid. Consistent with the winter baseline period, Cluster 2 (morning heating startup) dominates with 114114 occurrences, followed by Cluster 3 (unpowered thermal surge, 4949 occurrences) and Cluster 1 (autumn moisture disturbance, 33 occurrences). Because routing uses cluster radii rather than a score cutoff, predict_stream() also captures sub-threshold occurrences of known faults (such as Cluster 3 with a median score of 0.5490.549). Cluster 4 records zero matches because its baseline singleton radius is R4=0R_4 = 0.
  • Novel Anomaly (1717 occurrences): Seventeen observations exceed T=0.60T = 0.60 (median score 0.6430.643, maximum 0.6840.684) while falling outside the radius of every baseline medoid (median distance 0.7460.746).

6.2 Isolating and Clustering Novel Anomalies

Rather than pooling historical and streaming anomalies together—which allows frequent faults like Cluster 2 to dominate the distance matrix—we keep the locked baseline archetypes and pass stream_routed directly to method isolate_novel_anomalies().

This method branches engine_baseline onto the 1717Novel Anomaly observations, computes their pairwise Hamming distances using the frozen baseline forest, selects the optimal number of novel sub-clusters via DIANA and global silhouette width, extracts their ±2\pm 2-hour medoid windows, and commits a dedicated ledger.

Figure 31 shows how the four novel sub-clusters compare to the baseline archetypes:

  • Novel Archetype 1 (n=6n = 6): Exhibits a one-hour surge in power (0→5 kW0 \to 5\text{ kW}) and energy accompanied by opposing temperature shifts. Unlike a normal heating cycle, t_supply dips from 30∘C30^\circ\text{C} to 24∘C24^\circ\text{C} (with a spike in rh_supply) while t_return rises from 18∘C18^\circ\text{C} to 21∘C21^\circ\text{C} before reverting when power returns to zero.
  • Novel Archetype 2 (n=3n = 3): Resembles Baseline Archetype 3 in that t_supply surges from 17∘C17^\circ\text{C} to 30∘C30^\circ\text{C} (driving rh_supply down from 45%45\% to 30%30\%) while power and energy remain near zero. Here, however, the surge is sustained and followed by oscillations in t_saturation (17∘C–21∘C17^\circ\text{C}\text{--}21^\circ\text{C}).
  • Novel Archetypes 3 (n=6n = 6) and 4 (n=2n = 2): Both show a sustained step-up in power (0→5 kW0 \to 5\text{ kW}) and energy at t=0t = 0, similar to Baseline Archetype 2. However, whereas Baseline Archetype 2 drove simultaneous increases in t_supply and t_return, here t_supply and t_saturation drop at t=0t = 0—sharply in Novel Archetype 3 (sp_return ≈19.5∘C\approx 19.5^\circ\text{C}, with t_saturation falling from 19∘C19^\circ\text{C} to 14∘C14^\circ\text{C}) and more moderately in Novel Archetype 4 (sp_return ≈21.5∘C\approx 21.5^\circ\text{C}, preceded by a ramp in rh_return).

To identify the engineered features separating these four novel fault modes—particularly Novel Archetypes 3 and 4—we run ablate_features() on engine_novel.

Run LOCO Ablation on Novel Medoids

Plot Code

  novel_ablation_results,

The LOCO ablation results (Figure 32) clarify the feature drivers behind each novel sub-cluster:

  • Novel Cluster 1: Driven by rapid changes in return temperature (d_t_return_15m) and humidity (d_humidity_delta_15m) coupled with power and energy (dw_power, dw_energy). Whereas Baseline Archetype 1 was an unpowered moisture disturbance, this fault pairs a moisture and return-air transient with a brief power pulse.
  • Novel Cluster 2: Contains no power or energy features among its top five drivers. Unlike Baseline Archetype 3—which was driven by 15-minute thermal step changes—Novel Cluster 2 is dominated by cumulative multi-step displacements (displacement_supply_margin, t_sup_displacement, displacement_humidity_delta), capturing the sustained thermal ramp and saturation instability.
  • Novel Cluster 3 vs. Novel Cluster 4: Although both are led by dw_power (and include dw_energy), their secondary drivers explain why DIANA separates them:
    • Novel Cluster 3 is driven by return-saturation margins: ranks 2, 3, and 4 consist of d_return_margin_15m, displacement_return_margin, and return_margin, reflecting the 5∘C5^\circ\text{C} drop in t_saturation relative to t_return at startup.
    • Novel Cluster 4 is driven by humidity-delta kinematics (d_humidity_delta_15m at rank 2 and run_length_humidity_delta at rank 5) alongside d_return_margin_15m (rank 3), capturing the two-hour climb in rh_return (18%→27%18\% \to 27\%) relative to rh_supply prior to the power surge.

Combining the trajectory profiles (Figure 31) with the LOCO feature rankings (Figure 32) suggests the following physical interpretations for the four novel fault modes:

  • Novel Cluster 1 (Economizer or Outdoor-Air Damper Transient): A one-hour power pulse occurs alongside a drop in t_supply (30∘C→24∘C30^\circ\text{C} \to 24^\circ\text{C}) and a rise in t_return (18∘C→21∘C18^\circ\text{C} \to 21^\circ\text{C}). This pattern might represent an economizer or outdoor-air damper opening in response to rising indoor return temperatures (d_t_return_15m), drawing in cooler, more humid autumn air (d_humidity_delta_15m) while the supply fan powers up to flush the zone.
  • Novel Cluster 2 (Sustained Heating Valve Leak): Whereas Baseline Archetype 3 captured brief unpowered thermal spikes, Novel Cluster 2 could reflect a heating coil valve stuck partially open over multiple hours. In this scenario, hot water continues to heat the supply air (t_sup_displacement, displacement_supply_margin) while electrical power remains off, triggering downstream oscillations in t_saturation.
  • Novel Cluster 3 (Mechanical Cooling or Defrost Engagement): A sharp power step-up is paired with an immediate drop in both t_supply and t_saturation (19∘C→14∘C19^\circ\text{C} \to 14^\circ\text{C}) at a lower return setpoint (sp_return ≈19.5∘C\approx 19.5^\circ\text{C}). Rather than a winter heating startup (Baseline Archetype 2), this could reflect compressor-driven cooling or a heat-pump defrost cycle that rapidly chills the coil below the return-air temperature (d_return_margin_15m, displacement_return_margin).
  • Novel Cluster 4 (Latent Occupancy Load / Dehumidification Startup): Preceded by a steady two-hour climb in rh_return (18%→27%18\% \to 27\%) at a higher setpoint (sp_return ≈21.5∘C\approx 21.5^\circ\text{C}), the unit powers on (dw_power), likely to address accumulated indoor moisture (d_humidity_delta_15m, run_length_humidity_delta), producing a milder drop in t_supply and t_saturation as moisture condenses across the coil.

7 Turin HVAC Case Study: Key Findings

Applying the isoRouting pipeline to the Turin HVAC telemetry dataset demonstrated how an unsupervised Isolation Forest can be turned into an interpretable, end-to-end fault routing system. Across the pre-gap baseline and post-gap streaming periods, the analysis yielded four main findings:

  • Feature Dilution vs. Signal Drivers: Adding 6 mode-dwell counters to the 24 thermodynamic and control features compressed the upper tail of the anomaly score distribution rather than sharpening it (Figure 12, Figure 13). A subsequent leave-one-out audit confirmed that 20 of the 24 retained features actively drive high anomaly scores (Figure 21). Because forest scoring is fast and DiagnosticEngine decouples feature selection into external YAML files, auditing and swapping feature sets required no changes to the downstream pipeline.
  • Validated Multimodal Fault Regimes: On the pre-gap baseline telemetry, varying candidate anomaly thresholds revealed a clear operating regime where extracted anomalies separated into k=4k = 4 distinct, low-dimensional clusters. evaluate_k_stability() (Figure 23) alongside the Monte Carlo null controls in simulate_dip_control() (Figure 24) and simulate_lid_control() (Figure 25) provided quantitative bounds to select both the score cutoff and the number of baseline clusters (kk).
  • Interpretable Physical Archetypes: Partitioning the baseline tail by leaf-sharing Hamming distance summarized thousands of timestamps into a compact set of concrete historical trajectories (extract_medoids(), Figure 26) logged via commit_ledger(). Leave-One-Covariate-Out ablation (ablate_features(), Figure 27) linked each archetype directly to its driving physical channels—such as supply/return temperature displacements and control margins—turning abstract anomaly scores into actionable root-cause profiles.
  • Precursor Tracking and Emerging Post-Gap Faults: Caching the baseline medoid signatures (@baseline_signatures) and cluster radii (@cluster_radii) enabled immediate classification of additional telemetry without retraining the forest. route_time_course() revealed sub-threshold precursors leading into major events (Figure 30), while predict_stream() triaged post-gap telemetry into normal operation, recurring baseline archetypes, and out-of-distribution events (Table 6). Branching a secondary engine onto the rejected events via isolate_novel_anomalies() showed that the post-gap novelties were four new emerging fault regimes (Table 7, Figure 31, Figure 32).
